newsitem.title: USA: HMOs triple fees for doctor visits.
newsitem.headline: HMOs triple fees for doctor visits.

text.p: Health maintenance organisations (HMOs) have changed dramatically as they have grown in the past decade, including tripling fees patients pay to see a doctor, a researcher said on Saturday.

Fees paid for doctor visits are still relatively low, but have risen from $1.18 in 1987 to $4.51 in 1993. For a hospital stay, the fee or co-payment per day rose from $4.50 to $24.90, according to the report in the journal Health Affairs by researcher Jon Gabel.

He cited a study at Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound that found that imposing a $5 copay for a doctor's visit that had previosuly been free led to a decrease in the number of visits to a doctor.
The report also attributed the increase in copays to the rise of for-profit HMOs and the diminishing number of nonprofit ones.
From 1990-95 the number of Americans enrolled in HMOs soared, from 36.5 million to 58.2 million.
Most of the data in the journal article came from two surveys by the HMO industry.
Other changes in the managed care industry include fewer free-standing HMO centres with their own offices and facilities and more HMOs based on contractual relations with various doctors.

More managed care groups are also offering a combination of traditional HMOs and other forms of managed care where people have other options for seeing doctors of their own choice for additional fees.
